title: Cost Modelling and Total Cost of Ownership
objectives: Build accurate cost models that inform architecture decisions
Calculate Total Cost of Ownership across the full service lifecycle
Apply the Green Book's approach to option appraisal using whole-life costs
Distinguish between capital expenditure, operational expenditure, and transition costs
Present cost models that investment committees can use to make funding decisions
whyThisMatters:
Architecture decisions are investment decisions. Every technology choice, every platform selection, every integration approach has a cost that extends far beyond the initial build. A system that is cheap to build but expensive to operate may cost more over five years than one that is expensive to build but cheap to run. An architecture that saves money today but creates lock-in costs far more when the contract is renegotiated.

In government, where public money must be spent wisely and is subject to scrutiny, the ability to model costs accurately is essential. The HM Treasury Green Book (updated 2026) requires whole-life costing for business cases. Investment committees expect to see Total Cost of Ownership spanning the full appraisal period — typically 5-10 years for technology. The Digital Assurance Playbook checks whether initiatives represent good value.

Architects who cannot model costs accurately lose influence over investment decisions. Their technical recommendations are overridden by financial analysis from people who do not understand the technology. Architects who can demonstrate the financial implications of their decisions — in terms that finance directors understand — retain the influence to shape how public money is spent on technology.

content.heading: Total Cost of Ownership: The Full Picture
content.body:
Total Cost of Ownership (TCO) is the complete cost of a technology solution across its entire lifecycle — from initial investment through operations, maintenance, evolution, and eventual decommissioning. It is the number that determines whether an architecture decision represents good value for public money.

TCO includes categories that architects frequently underestimate:

Capital expenditure (CapEx): one-time costs to build or acquire the solution. Includes: development effort (internal or contracted), platform/product licensing (one-time), infrastructure provisioning, data migration from legacy systems, security testing and assessment, and initial training for the team.

Operational expenditure (OpEx): ongoing costs to run the solution. Includes: cloud hosting costs (compute, storage, data transfer, managed services), annual licensing fees, support contracts, operational staff (or proportion of shared operational team), monitoring and tooling, security patching and vulnerability management, and regular backup and DR testing.

Evolution expenditure: costs to keep the solution current and adapt it to changing needs. Includes: feature development (responding to policy changes, user needs), technology refresh (upgrading frameworks, updating dependencies), scalability investment (growing capacity as demand increases), and accessibility improvements (meeting evolving WCAG standards).

Transition costs: costs of moving from the current state to the new solution. Includes: data migration (extraction, transformation, loading, validation), dual running (operating old and new simultaneously during transition), user transition (training, change management, communication), integration rework (connecting existing systems to the new solution), and decommissioning the old system (data archiving, contract termination, infrastructure removal).

Exit costs: costs of eventually leaving the solution. These are often forgotten but significant. Includes: data extraction from the platform, migration to a replacement, contract termination fees, knowledge transition, and decommissioning infrastructure.

A common architect mistake: presenting the build cost as the investment decision. 'This will cost £2 million to build' tells the investment committee nothing useful without also knowing the annual operational cost (£500,000? £50,000?), the expected lifetime (3 years? 10 years?), and the transition costs (£200,000 for data migration? £2 million for decommissioning legacy?). The TCO over 5 years might be £2 million or £7 million depending on these factors.

content.heading: Cloud Cost Modelling: FinOps Principles for Government
content.body:
Cloud computing fundamentally changes cost modelling. Instead of large upfront capital purchases (servers, storage, networking equipment), cloud costs are operational — you pay for what you use, when you use it. This creates both opportunity (scale down when demand is low) and risk (unexpected costs from usage spikes or misconfigured services).

Cloud cost categories for government services:

Compute costs: the processing power running your applications. In containerised environments, this is typically priced by vCPU and memory allocation per hour. Costs scale with the number of instances and their size. Auto-scaling can reduce costs during low-demand periods but requires careful configuration to avoid over-provisioning.

Storage costs: data at rest. Pricing varies dramatically by storage tier — high-performance SSD storage costs 10-20x more than archive storage. Architecture decisions about data lifecycle (when does data move from hot to cold storage?) directly affect cost.

Data transfer costs: moving data between services, between regions, and out of the cloud provider. These are often the most surprising cloud costs. An architecture with chatty inter-service communication or large data transfers between regions can accumulate significant transfer costs that were not in the original estimate.

Managed service costs: databases, message queues, AI services, monitoring — managed services have their own pricing models, often based on throughput, storage, or request count. These can be cost-effective (no operational staff needed) or expensive (pricing at scale) depending on usage patterns.

FinOps principles for government:

Visibility: tag all cloud resources by service, team, and environment. This enables cost attribution — knowing which service costs what, and spotting anomalies quickly.

Optimisation: regularly review resource utilisation. Right-size instances (many teams over-provision for safety). Use reserved capacity or savings plans for predictable baseline workloads. Delete unused resources (test environments left running, old storage not cleaned up).

Governance: set budgets and alerts. Unexpected cost increases often indicate misconfiguration or security incidents (crypto-mining on compromised instances is not uncommon). Alert when costs exceed expected thresholds.

Forecasting: model future costs based on demand projections. If user numbers are growing 20% per year, cloud costs will grow similarly (unless you optimise). Include growth projections in your TCO model.

content.heading: Comparing Options: The Green Book Approach
content.body:
The HM Treasury Green Book (2026 edition) provides the government's framework for comparing investment options. For architects presenting options to investment committees, the key concepts are:

Whole-life costs: compare options over the full appraisal period (typically 5-10 years for technology). Do not compare build costs alone — compare total lifecycle costs including operations, maintenance, and evolution. An option that is £500,000 cheaper to build but £200,000 more expensive to operate annually is more expensive over any period longer than 2.5 years.

Discounting: the Green Book requires future costs and benefits to be discounted to present values using the Treasury discount rate. This reflects the time value of money — a cost incurred in year 5 is worth less in today's terms than the same cost incurred in year 1. The finance team handles the discounting calculation, but you must provide the raw annual cost profiles accurately.

Optimism bias: the Green Book requires cost estimates to be adjusted upward to account for the well-documented tendency to underestimate costs. For standard technology projects, an optimism bias uplift of 10-25% is typical at Outline Business Case stage (reducing as the project matures and estimates become more certain). Be honest about where your estimates are least certain — that is where optimism bias should be highest.

Counterfactual comparison: always include a 'do nothing' or 'do minimum' option showing what happens if the investment is not made. This is not zero cost — the do-nothing option has ongoing costs (maintenance, workarounds, inefficiency, risk) that often exceed the cost of investment. Quantifying the do-nothing cost is often the strongest argument for investment.

Sensitivity analysis: show how the comparison changes under different assumptions. What if demand grows 50% faster than projected? What if the vendor increases prices by 30%? What if the project takes 6 months longer? Sensitivity analysis gives the committee confidence that the recommendation is robust — or reveals that it is fragile and depends on specific assumptions being correct.

Value for money is not the same as lowest cost. The Green Book looks for best value — the option that provides the greatest net benefit when costs, benefits, risks, and strategic alignment are all considered. A more expensive option may be better value if it delivers greater benefits, carries less risk, or better aligns with strategy.

content.heading: Common Cost Modelling Mistakes
content.body:
Government technology cost models fail in predictable ways. Recognising these patterns helps you build more accurate models.

Forgetting operational costs: the most common failure. A cost model that shows £2 million build cost without mentioning the £600,000 annual operational cost is misleading. For cloud-native services, operational costs often exceed build costs within 2-3 years. Always model the full lifecycle.

Ignoring people costs: technology does not run itself. Someone must: deploy changes, respond to incidents, manage security patches, handle user support escalations, and make configuration changes when policy evolves. If the answer is 'the development team does this,' include their ongoing cost. If the answer is 'we will need an operations team,' include their recruitment and salary costs.

Underestimating integration costs: connecting your new system to existing departmental systems is almost always more expensive and time-consuming than expected. Legacy systems have undocumented interfaces, inconsistent data formats, and limited capacity for new connections. Budget at least 20-30% of build cost for integration.

Ignoring transition costs: data migration, dual running, user training, and decommissioning the old system are significant costs that are frequently omitted from business cases. For major system replacements, transition costs can be 30-50% of the build cost.

Comparing cloud and on-premise incorrectly: cloud costs are operational (ongoing). On-premise costs are heavily capital (upfront hardware plus ongoing staff). Comparing year-1 costs favours on-premise (no ongoing hosting fees). Comparing 5-year TCO often favours cloud (no hardware refresh, no data centre costs, reduced staffing). Always compare over the same timeframe.

Assuming fixed vendor pricing: vendor pricing changes — usually upward. Build annual price increases into your model (5-10% per year is a reasonable assumption for commercial software). If the vendor controls your pricing and you have no alternative (lock-in), model the risk of significant price increases.

Forgetting the cost of delay: not starting now has a cost. If the current system costs £1 million per year in maintenance and the new system would cost £300,000, every year you delay costs £700,000 in unnecessary maintenance. Include this 'cost of inaction' in your comparison.

content.heading: Presenting Cost Models to Investment Committees
content.body:
Investment committees make funding decisions based on cost models. How you present your model determines whether it is trusted and acted upon.

Use annual cost profiles: show costs year by year across the appraisal period. This reveals the investment pattern — high capital in years 1-2, reducing to steady-state operational cost in years 3-5. Committees want to see when money is needed and how much, aligned with budget planning cycles.

Separate CapEx from OpEx: government budgets often have separate capital and revenue allocations. Capital budgets fund one-time investments. Revenue budgets fund ongoing operations. Your model must show which costs fall in which category so the committee can assess affordability against both budgets.

Show cumulative cost comparison: for option comparison, show cumulative TCO over time. This reveals the crossover point — when a higher-build-cost option becomes cheaper than a lower-build-cost option due to lower ongoing costs. A graph showing cumulative cost curves for each option is highly effective.

Include a cost breakdown by component: show where the money goes. Infrastructure: X%. Development: Y%. Licensing: Z%. This allows the committee to challenge specific assumptions ('is that licensing cost correct? Have you negotiated?') and understand what drives the total.

State your assumptions explicitly: every cost model depends on assumptions (demand projections, pricing stability, team productivity, timeline). List your key assumptions and state what happens to the cost model if they are wrong. This builds trust — a model that claims certainty is less credible than one that acknowledges uncertainty.

Include confidence levels: for each major cost line, indicate your confidence in the estimate. High confidence: based on actual quotes or historical data. Medium confidence: based on analogous projects or industry benchmarks. Low confidence: based on expert judgement with limited comparable data. This helps the committee understand where the model is robust and where additional investigation might be warranted.

The finance team is your ally: work with your programme's finance business partner to validate your model against their expectations. They know how investment committees think, what format they expect, and what questions they will ask. A cost model co-produced with finance is far more credible than one produced by a technologist alone.

workedExample.title: TCO Comparison: Build vs Buy for a Document Management System
workedExample.context: DESNZ needs a document management capability for 500 internal staff handling 5 million compliance documents. The architect must compare: Option A (build a custom solution on cloud infrastructure) versus Option B (procure a commercial SaaS document management platform) versus Option C (extend an existing departmental platform that currently handles a different document type). The investment committee needs a 5-year TCO comparison.
workedExample.approach:
The architect builds a detailed cost model for each option over 5 years.

Option A — Custom Build:
Year 1: £1.2M (8 developers × 12 months @ £12.5K/month average blended rate + infrastructure setup + security testing)
Year 2: £450K (4 developers ongoing feature work + cloud hosting £80K + operational support)
Year 3-5: £350K/year (2 developers maintenance + hosting growth + security patching)
5-year TCO: £2,700K
Risks: delivery timeline risk, ongoing maintenance burden, recruitment for specialist skills.

Option B — SaaS Procurement:
Year 1: £380K (implementation partner £250K + first year licence £130K for 500 users)
Year 2-5: £165K/year (licence £130K + annual support/configuration changes £35K)
5-year TCO: £1,040K
Risks: vendor lock-in (proprietary format), 5% annual licence increase assumed, limited customisation.

Option C — Extend Existing Platform:
Year 1: £550K (4 developers × 9 months for new document type support + data migration from legacy stores)
Year 2-5: £120K/year (shared operational cost allocation + 1 developer for ongoing support)
5-year TCO: £1,030K
Risks: existing platform is already at 80% capacity, extension adds complexity for the existing team, shared governance with the other user group.

Transition costs (applicable to all): £200K for data migration from legacy document stores (consistent across options).

The architect presents the comparison with sensitivity analysis: if Option B licence costs increase 10% annually instead of 5%, its 5-year TCO rises to £1,180K — still cheaper than Option A but now comparable to Option C. If Option C requires platform capacity expansion (likely), add £150K in year 2.
workedExample.outcome: The investment committee selects Option C (extend existing platform) as best value, with a condition: the architect must assess platform capacity and confirm the extension is technically feasible before committing. The committee notes that Option B is a viable fallback if Option C proves infeasible. Option A is rejected on cost grounds despite offering the most flexibility. The architect records the decision as an ADR with full cost rationale.
workedExample.lessonsLearned: The TCO comparison revealed that the cheapest build cost (Option B at £380K year 1) and the cheapest total cost (Option C at £1,030K over 5 years) were different options — demonstrating why whole-life costing matters. Option A was the most expensive by nearly 3x despite giving the most control — the investment committee judged that control was not worth the premium for a generic capability like document management. Including the sensitivity analysis (what if licence costs increase faster?) gave the committee confidence that Option C remained competitive even under pessimistic assumptions.

civilServiceScenario.title: The Cloud Bill That Shocked the Finance Director
civilServiceScenario.background: A department migrated 5 services to the cloud 18 months ago. The business case estimated annual cloud costs at £180,000. The actual bill for the last 12 months was £520,000 — nearly triple the estimate. The finance director is demanding an explanation and considering whether to move back to on-premise (where costs were 'predictable'). The overrun has consumed budget intended for a new service development, which is now unfunded.
civilServiceScenario.challenge: As the Solution Architect, you must: (1) identify why costs exceeded estimates, (2) propose optimisation that brings costs closer to the original estimate, and (3) advise whether moving back to on-premise is the right response.
constraints: The actual cloud bill breakdown: compute 40%, storage 25%, data transfer 20%, managed services 15%
Non-production environments (dev, test, staging) are running 24/7 at production specification
Auto-scaling is configured but minimum instance counts are set too high
Large volumes of data transfer between services in different regions (an early architecture decision)
Storage is accumulating because no retention policy is enforced — old data is never archived or deleted
The original cost estimate was based on a vendor's pricing calculator without realistic usage patterns
The department does not have cloud cost monitoring or alerting
Moving back to on-premise would require capital investment of £800,000 plus ongoing data centre costs
Three of the five services have grown in usage by 40% since migration
civilServiceScenario.yourRole: You are the Solution Architect advising the finance director and proposing a cost optimisation strategy.
civilServiceScenario.discussion:
This scenario is common in government cloud migrations. The causes are typically: over-provisioned non-production environments (easy fix — schedule them to shut down outside working hours or right-size them), minimum instance counts set for worst-case rather than typical load (reduce minimums, trust auto-scaling), data transfer between regions (architecture decision that should have been caught in design — colocate services that communicate frequently), and storage accumulation without lifecycle management (implement retention policies).

The architect should: implement immediate cost reduction (non-production scheduling and right-sizing can reduce costs 30-40% with no service impact), address the cross-region data transfer (relocate services to the same region — a bigger change but addresses 20% of the bill), implement storage lifecycle management (archive old data, delete expired data), and set up cost monitoring and alerting (so costs never drift this far without detection again).

Moving back to on-premise is almost certainly the wrong answer — the £800,000 capital plus ongoing data centre costs likely exceeds the optimised cloud costs, and you lose the scaling and resilience benefits. But the architect must demonstrate this with a fair comparison rather than asserting it.

practiceArtefact.description: Build a 5-year TCO model comparing two options for a government service hosting 200,000 citizen records: Option A (managed cloud platform with SaaS components) versus Option B (self-hosted on government cloud infrastructure with open source components). Include all cost categories: capital, operational, people, transition, and evolution.
practiceArtefact.guidance: Consider: cloud hosting costs grow with data volume and user numbers. SaaS licensing grows with user count. Self-hosted requires operations staff. Both options need security maintenance. Include realistic growth assumptions (15% per year in data volume, 10% per year in users). Present as an annual cost profile and cumulative comparison.
practiceArtefact.modelAnswer:
**5-Year TCO Comparison: Managed Platform vs Self-Hosted**

Assumptions: 200,000 initial records, growing 15%/year. 500 initial staff users, growing 10%/year. Data volume: 2TB initial, growing 15%/year.

**Option A — Managed Cloud Platform (SaaS components)**

| Category | Y1 | Y2 | Y3 | Y4 | Y5 | Total |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| SaaS licence (per user) | £130K | £143K | £157K | £173K | £190K | £793K |
| Cloud hosting (data, compute) | £65K | £75K | £86K | £99K | £114K | £439K |
| Implementation/configuration | £250K | £0 | £0 | £0 | £0 | £250K |
| Ongoing configuration changes | £35K | £35K | £40K | £40K | £45K | £195K |
| Security & compliance | £20K | £20K | £20K | £20K | £20K | £100K |
| **Annual total** | **£500K** | **£273K** | **£303K** | **£332K** | **£369K** | **£1,777K** |

**Option B — Self-Hosted (open source components)**

| Category | Y1 | Y2 | Y3 | Y4 | Y5 | Total |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Development (build) | £800K | £200K | £0 | £0 | £0 | £1,000K |
| Cloud infrastructure | £48K | £55K | £63K | £73K | £84K | £323K |
| Operations team (2 FTE) | £160K | £165K | £170K | £175K | £180K | £850K |
| Ongoing development (1 FTE) | £0 | £80K | £82K | £85K | £87K | £334K |
| Security & patching | £30K | £35K | £40K | £45K | £50K | £200K |
| **Annual total** | **£1,038K** | **£535K** | **£355K** | **£378K** | **£401K** | **£2,707K** |

**Cumulative TCO:**
- Option A: Y1 £500K, Y2 £773K, Y3 £1,076K, Y4 £1,408K, Y5 £1,777K
- Option B: Y1 £1,038K, Y2 £1,573K, Y3 £1,928K, Y4 £2,306K, Y5 £2,707K

**Analysis:** Option A is cheaper at every point in the 5-year period. The gap is largest in Year 1 (Option B has high build cost) and narrows slightly as Option A's licence costs grow. Option A's 5-year TCO is £930K less than Option B.

**Sensitivity:** If SaaS licence increases are 15%/year (not 10%), Option A 5-year TCO rises to £2,050K — still £657K cheaper than Option B. Option B only becomes cheaper than A if the SaaS licence grows 25%+ annually — unlikely for an established product.

**Recommendation:** Option A (managed platform) is clearly better value unless there are non-financial reasons to prefer Option B (vendor lock-in concerns, specific customisation needs that SaaS cannot support). Record rationale in ADR.

reflectiveQuestions: Think about the last technology investment your department made. Was the cost model accurate over time? What was underestimated?
Do your architecture options papers include whole-life costs, or do they focus primarily on build costs? What difference would full TCO make to the recommendation?
Has your department experienced unexpected cloud cost increases? What caused them, and what architecture decisions would have prevented them?
How do you model the cost of inaction — the ongoing expense of not modernising or not investing? Is this included in your business cases?
When was the last time a cost model you produced was challenged by the finance team? What did they see that you missed?

knowledgeCheck.question: What is Total Cost of Ownership (TCO)?
options: The upfront cost of building or buying a solution
The complete cost across the entire lifecycle including build, operation, evolution, and decommissioning
The annual operational budget for a service
The cost of the technology components only, excluding people
knowledgeCheck.explanation: TCO encompasses all costs across the full lifecycle: capital expenditure (build/acquire), operational expenditure (run), evolution expenditure (maintain and improve), transition costs (migrate to the new solution), and exit costs (eventually leave the solution). It is the number that determines whether an investment represents good value for money.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is the most commonly underestimated cost category in government technology projects?
options: Software licensing costs
Ongoing operational costs including people, hosting, and maintenance
Initial development costs
Hardware procurement costs
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Architects consistently underestimate operational costs — the ongoing expense of running a service after it is built. This includes hosting costs (which grow with usage), people costs (operations, support, ongoing development), security maintenance, and the cost of responding to policy changes. For cloud services, operational costs often exceed build costs within 2-3 years.

knowledgeCheck.question: According to the Green Book, what is optimism bias?
options: The tendency for architects to recommend the most expensive option
The well-documented tendency to underestimate costs and overestimate benefits in project appraisals
A positive attitude toward technology adoption
The belief that cloud computing is always cheaper than on-premise
knowledgeCheck.explanation: The Green Book recognises that project cost estimates are systematically too low and benefit estimates too high — this is optimism bias. It requires cost estimates to be adjusted upward (10-25% for standard technology projects at OBC stage) to provide a more realistic picture for decision-makers.

knowledgeCheck.question: When comparing a cloud SaaS option against a self-hosted open source option, what timeframe typically reveals the true cost difference?
options: Year 1 only — the initial costs tell the full story
3-5 years — long enough for operational costs and growth to compound
10+ years — anything shorter is misleading
The comparison is meaningless because they are fundamentally different
knowledgeCheck.explanation: A 3-5 year comparison captures the full picture: SaaS has lower Year 1 cost (no build) but ongoing licence fees that grow with users. Self-hosted has higher Year 1 (build cost) but lower ongoing cost (no licence). The crossover point — where self-hosted becomes cheaper — typically occurs at 3-5 years if it occurs at all. Shorter comparisons favour SaaS; very long comparisons may favour self-hosted.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why is the 'do nothing' option important in a cost model?
options: It provides a baseline showing that doing nothing also has costs — maintenance, inefficiency, risk
It is required by procurement regulations but has no analytical purpose
It always shows zero cost, making other options look expensive by comparison
It is only needed if the investment committee is likely to reject the proposal
knowledgeCheck.explanation: The 'do nothing' option quantifies the cost of inaction — ongoing maintenance burden, operational inefficiency, growing technical debt, and accumulating risk. This is often the strongest argument for investment because it shows that NOT investing is not free — it costs money every year in maintenance, workarounds, and risk. A well-quantified 'do nothing' cost makes the investment case compelling.
